main_damage_causes: Collapse of Stan's characterisation in the theatrical Prisoner of Azkaban cut removes his personality, voice, and all the traits (nosiness, excitability, folk-fear of Voldemort) that make him a recognisable recurring presence
Absence of Goblet of Fire and Order of the Phoenix reappearances eliminates the relationship continuity that gives his wrongful arrest and Harry's defence of him any emotional resonance

Loss of the Stan-as-moral-touchstone arc (arrest, Harry vs Scrimgeour, Battle of the Seven Potters Disarm decision) degrades both Harry's characterisation as a defender of ordinary people and the Ministry-injustice theme from a concrete human example to an abstract one

damaging_scenes.scene: Prisoner of Azkaban - Knight Bus arrival and ride (theatrical)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Stan is characterised as dropping his 'professional manner' quickly, sniggering at Harry, asking nosy questions about his scar, and showing genuine curiosity and a cheeky, lively personality. He engages Harry in extended conversation about Sirius Black, reacts with full-body terror when Harry says Voldemort's name (pimples going white), and is an active, talkative presence throughout the ride.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The theatrical release strips out the extended Knight Bus ride (shrunken head sequence excluded per non-theatrical note). Stan's conversational role is drastically reduced. The Voldemort-name reaction, the Sirius Black discussion, and Stan's gossipy, excitable personality are all absent or collapsed. Stan becomes a largely functional, dreary presence who ushers Harry aboard and little more.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book establishes Stan's defining personality traits — his nosiness, his working-class cheek, his excitability, his fear of Voldemort's name — almost entirely through the Knight Bus ride. With the extended ride cut from theatrical release, virtually all of this characterisation is lost. The audience receives no sense of who Stan is beyond a perfunctory conductor, making his later appearances (arrest, Battle of the Seven Potters) meaningless to film-only viewers.

damaging_scenes.scene: Prisoner of Azkaban - Knight Bus arrival and ride (theatrical)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Stan asks Harry's name, suspects something is off, and notices the scar — a moment of suspense where Harry must quickly lie ('Neville Longbottom'). Stan's suspicious, probing nature is part of a brief cat-and-mouse dynamic that establishes Harry's vulnerability and Stan's street-level perceptiveness.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film retains 'Wot you say your name was again?' / 'I didn't.' as a brief exchange, but the scar-noticing, the suspicion, and the 'Neville Longbottom' alias are absent. The identity-concealment beat is dropped entirely.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The alias 'Neville Longbottom' is a small but characterful moment — it shows Harry's quick thinking under pressure and Stan's inquisitive nature. Its loss is minor in isolation but contributes to the overall flattening of Stan's personality in the theatrical cut.

damaging_scenes.scene: Prisoner of Azkaban - Knight Bus arrival and ride (theatrical)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Stan reacts with full-body panic when Harry accidentally says 'Voldemort' — his pimples go white, Ernie jerks the wheel — and then recovers, clutching his chest. This is both comic and characterising: Stan is excitable, superstitious, and deeply embedded in wizarding folk-fear of the Dark Lord.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: This scene does not appear in the theatrical film corpus. The Voldemort-name reaction is entirely absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The Voldemort-name reaction is one of the most vivid and funny Stan moments in the books and encapsulates the ordinary wizarding world's terror of the name. Its loss removes a key beat that both characterises Stan and contextualises the broader wizarding culture of fear.

damaging_scenes.scene: Deathly Hallows Part 1 - Snatchers capture scene
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Ron uses 'Stan Shunpike' as an alias because Stan is the first person who comes to mind — a small but meaningful callback that reflects Stan's continued presence in the trio's consciousness, and the Snatchers confirm they know Stan personally ('We know Stan Shunpike, 'e's put a bit of work our way'), revealing Stan has been doing work for the Death Eater-aligned Snatchers, complicating his earlier arrest narrative.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film retains Ron saying 'Stan Shunpike' and Scabior saying 'Like 'ell you are. We know skinny Stan. Try again.' The Snatchers' knowledge of Stan is present but the specific detail that Stan 'has put a bit of work our way' is absent from the film corpus, removing the implication that Stan has actively collaborated with Snatchers.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book line 'he's put a bit of work our way' adds a layer of moral ambiguity to Stan's Imperius/arrest storyline — suggesting he may have been actively used by Death Eater forces. The film drops this, leaving Stan's mention as a throwaway gag rather than a meaningful narrative thread. For film-only viewers who have no investment in Stan, the reference lands as near-meaningless regardless.

damaging_scenes.scene: Goblet of Fire / Order of the Phoenix - Stan at the Quidditch World Cup and aboard the Knight Bus (book material absent from film entirely)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book reintroduces Stan at the Quidditch World Cup, showing him under veela influence boasting he will 'become the youngest ever Minister of Magic' — a humorous callback that deepens his character as a lovable braggart and situates him in the wider wizarding community. Later in Order of the Phoenix he reappears on the Knight Bus and greets Harry warmly, fascinated by his fame.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Stan does not appear in the Goblet of Fire or Order of the Phoenix films at all. These appearances are entirely absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Stan's reappearances between Prisoner of Azkaban and Half-Blood Prince are what transform him from a one-scene background character into a recurring presence whose wrongful arrest carries emotional weight. Without Goblet of Fire's veela scene (which Ron later references when discussing Stan's arrest: 'Isn't he the one who claimed he was going to become Minister of Magic?') and Order of the Phoenix's warm reunion, the film audience has no relationship with Stan by the time he is arrested. His arrest in Half-Blood Prince and Harry's repeated championing of him in that film and Deathly Hallows land with zero impact for film viewers.

damaging_scenes.scene: Half-Blood Prince / Deathly Hallows - Stan's arrest and Harry's repeated defence of him
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Stan's wrongful arrest becomes a recurring moral touchstone. Harry invokes Stan's imprisonment directly to Scrimgeour (twice) as evidence of Ministry injustice, and Dumbledore has personally appealed for Stan's release. This arc makes Stan a symbol of institutional overreach and Harry's principled resistance to the Ministry, tying into core saga themes.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film corpus contains no Half-Blood Prince scenes involving Stan's arrest or Harry confronting Scrimgeour about it. Without the preceding reappearances (see above) and with Stan having been reduced to a near-ciphered figure in Prisoner of Azkaban, this entire moral arc is absent from the film adaptation.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is the most structurally damaging loss. In the books Stan functions as a low-stakes but emotionally clear example of Ministry injustice — an ordinary, harmless person sacrificed for appearances. Harry's willingness to challenge Scrimgeour repeatedly over Stan (rather than, say, a named hero) shows the depth of his moral conviction. The film strips this entirely, weakening Harry's characterisation as someone who fights for ordinary people and reducing the Ministry-as-villain arc to more abstract terms.

damaging_scenes.scene: Deathly Hallows Part 1 - Battle of the Seven Potters (not in film corpus but book corpus establishes it)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Harry recognises the Imperiused Stan Shunpike among the Death Eaters and chooses to Disarm rather than harm him, at near-fatal risk to himself. Lupin later rebukes Harry for this, and Harry insists 'So you think I should have killed Stan Shunpike?' This moment crystallises Harry's moral identity: he refuses to treat an innocent person as collateral damage even in mortal danger.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The Battle of the Seven Potters is depicted in Deathly Hallows Part 1 but the film corpus provided does not contain the Stan Shunpike recognition scene or Lupin's subsequent rebuke. Without any prior film relationship with Stan, even if the scene were present, it would carry no emotional weight for film audiences.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Harry's choice to spare Stan is one of the defining moral moments of Deathly Hallows — it nearly gets him killed, draws Voldemort's attention, and earns a direct argument with Lupin. It is inseparable from Stan's accumulated presence in the books. The film's failure to build Stan as a known, sympathetic figure means this moment (even if filmed) would be incomprehensible to film audiences: Harry risking death for someone they barely remember. The damage to Harry's moral characterisation and to the saga theme of protecting the innocent is significant.
